brontosaurus:enwiki:4.title: Brontosaurus (Second Dinosaur Rush and skull issue)

brontosaurus:enwiki:5.title: Brontosaurus (Skull correction, resurgent discoveries, and reassessment)

facts.statement: Brontosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic period, specifically from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian ages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Jurassic (Kimmeridgian to Tithonian),

facts.statement: The genus Brontosaurus was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1879.
facts.quote: authority: Marsh, 1879

facts.statement: The type species Brontosaurus excelsus was named based on a partial skeleton without a skull discovered in Como Bluff, Wyoming.
facts.quote: It was described by American paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh in 1879, the type species being dubbed B. excelsus, based on a partial skeleton lacking a skull found in Como Bluff, Wyoming.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus lived approximately 156 to 146 million years ago in the Morrison Formation of present-day Utah and Wyoming.
facts.quote: Brontosaurus lived about 156 to 146 million years ago (mya) during the Kimmeridgian and Tithonian ages in the Morrison Formation of what is now Utah and Wyoming.

facts.statement: A 2015 study by Emmanuel Tschopp and colleagues determined that Brontosaurus is a distinct genus rather than a synonym of Apatosaurus.
facts.quote: For decades, the animal was thought to have been a taxonomic synonym of its close relative Apatosaurus, but a 2015 study by Emmanuel Tschopp and colleagues found it to be distinct.

facts.statement: Fossils show that Brontosaurus was a large, quadrupedal dinosaur with a long neck and a tail ending in a whip-like structure.
facts.quote: The anatomy of Brontosaurus is well known, with fossils demonstrating that it was large, long-necked, and quadrupedal with a long tail terminating in a whip-like structure.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus possessed extremely robust and heavily built cervical vertebrae, unlike its lighter relatives Diplodocus and Barosaurus.
facts.quote: The cervical vertebrae are notably extremely robust and heavily built, in contrast to its lightly built relatives Diplodocus and Barosaurus.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus had short, stout forelimbs and elongated, thick hindlimbs supported by a heavy shoulder girdle and pelvis.
facts.quote: The forelimbs were short and stout whereas the hindlimbs were elongated and thick, supported respectively by a heavily built shoulder girdle and pelvis.

facts.statement: The largest species, B. excelsus, reached lengths of 21 to 23 meters and weighed 15 to 20 tonnes, while the smaller B. parvus grew up to 19 meters long.
facts.quote: Several size estimates have been made, with the largest species B. excelsus reaching up to 21 - 23 m from head to tail and weighing in at 15 - 20 t, whereas the smaller B. parvus only got up to 19 m long.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus belongs to the subfamily Apatosaurinae, a group containing only it and Apatosaurus, known for their firm builds and thick necks.
facts.quote: Brontosaurus is a genus in the subfamily Apatosaurinae, which includes only it and Apatosaurus, which are distinguished by their firm builds and thick necks.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Brontosaurus was collected from the Morrison Formation at Como Bluff, Wyoming, by William Harlow Reed.
facts.quote: The specimen was collected from Morrison Formation rocks at Como Bluff, Wyoming by William Harlow Reed.

facts.statement: Othniel Charles Marsh originally classified Brontosaurus within the clade Atlantosauridae, which he named in 1877 and included Atlantosaurus and Apatosaurus.
facts.quote: Marsh believed that Brontosaurus was a member of the Atlantosauridae, a clade of sauropod dinosaurs he named in 1877 that also included Atlantosaurus and Apatosaurus.

facts.statement: Research in 1998 and 2020 suggested that the skull Marsh attributed to Brontosaurus from the Felch Quarry actually belonged to Brachiosaurus.
facts.quote: In 1998, the Felch Quarry skull that Marsh included in his 1896 skeletal restoration was suggested to belong to Brachiosaurus instead and this was supported in 2020 with a redescription of the brachiosaurid material found at the Felch Quarry.

facts.statement: The taxonomic status of Brontosaurus remains debated, with some paleontologists still arguing it is a synonym of Apatosaurus.
facts.quote: However, the status of Brontosaurus is still uncertain, with some paleontologists still considering it a synonym of Apatosaurus.

facts.statement: A partial juvenile skeleton was collected by William Harlow Reed during a 1901 Carnegie Museum expedition in Wyoming.
facts.quote: During a Carnegie Museum expedition to Wyoming in 1901, William Harlow Reed collected another Brontosaurus skeleton, a partial postcranial skeleton of a young juvenile (CM 566), including partial limbs.

facts.statement: Olof A. Peterson and Charles Gilmore named the skeletons Elosaurus parvus in 1902.
facts.quote: The skeletons were granted a new genus and species name, Elosaurus parvus ("little field lizard"), by Olof A. Peterson and Charles Gilmore in 1902.

facts.statement: The juvenile and adult specimens were found in the Brushy Basin Member of the Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: Both of the specimens came from the Brushy Basin Member of the Morrison Formation.

facts.statement: The American Museum of Natural History unveiled the first mounted sauropod skeleton, named Brontosaurus excelsus, in 1905.
facts.quote: In 1905, the American Museum of Natural History (AMNH) unveiled the first-ever mounted skeleton of a sauropod, a composite specimen (mainly made of bones from AMNH 460) that they referred to as Brontosaurus excelsus.

facts.statement: An Apatosaurus skull was discovered in 1909 during Earl Douglass's first expedition to the Carnegie Quarry.
facts.quote: In 1909, an Apatosaurus skull was found, during the first expedition to what would become the Carnegie Quarry at Dinosaur National Monument, led by Earl Douglass.

facts.statement: After William J. Holland died in 1934, museum staff placed a Camarasaurus skull cast on the Carnegie Quarry mount.
facts.quote: After Holland's death in 1934, a cast of a Camarasaurus skull was placed on the mount by museum staff.

facts.statement: John Stanton McIntosh and David Berman redescribed Diplodocus and Apatosaurus skulls in 1975, noting similarities to Diplodocus.
facts.quote: No apatosaurine skull was mentioned in the literature until the 1970s when John Stanton McIntosh and David Berman redescribed the skulls of Diplodocus and Apatosaurus in 1975.

facts.statement: The first Apatosaurus skull was mounted on a skeleton at the Carnegie Museum on October 20, 1979.
facts.quote: On October 20, 1979, after the publications by McIntosh and Berman, the first skull of an Apatosaurus was mounted on a skeleton in a museum, that of the Carnegie.

facts.statement: The American Museum of Natural History remounted its skeleton in 1995 with a corrected tail and a skull cast from Apatosaurus louisae.
facts.quote: In 1995, the American Museum of Natural History followed suit, and unveiled their remounted skeleton (now labelled Apatosaurus excelsus) with a corrected tail and a new skull cast from A. louisae.

facts.statement: Robert T. Bakker referred a skull and mandible from Como Bluff to Brontosaurus excelsus in 1998, though the skull remains undescribed.
facts.quote: In 1998, Robert T. Bakker referred a skull and mandible of an apatosaurine from Como Bluff to Brontosaurus excelsus (TATE 099-01), though the skull is still undescribed.

facts.statement: The first Apatosaurus specimen with a skull articulated to its cervical vertebrae was described in 2011.
facts.quote: In 2011, the first specimen of Apatosaurus where a skull was found articulated with its cervical vertebrae was described.

facts.statement: A partial postcranial skeleton referred to Brontosaurus was discovered in 1993 in the Morrison Formation of central Wyoming.
facts.quote: Another specimen of an Apatosaurine now referred to Brontosaurus was discovered in 1993 by the Tate Geological Museum, also from the Morrison Formation of central Wyoming.

facts.statement: Several authors later transferred the species to the genus Apatosaurus.
facts.quote: The species was later transferred to Apatosaurus by several authors.

facts.statement: Emanuel Tschopp and colleagues placed the species in Brontosaurus in 2015.
facts.quote: The species was placed in Brontosaurus Tschopp et al. in 2015 during their comprehensive study of Diplodocidae.

facts.statement: A 2015 study by Tschopp, Mateus, and Benson concluded Brontosaurus is a valid genus distinct from Apatosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2015, an extensive study of diplodocid relationships by Emanuel Tschopp, Octavio Mateus, and Roger Benson concluded that Brontosaurus was indeed a valid genus of sauropod distinct from Apatosaurus.

facts.statement: Robert T. Bakker argued in the 1990s that Apatosaurus excelsus should remain a separate genus from Apatosaurus ajax.
facts.quote: Despite this, at least one paleontologist—Robert T. Bakker—argued in the 1990s that A. ajax and A. excelsus are sufficiently distinct that the latter continues to merit a separate genus.

facts.statement: Paleontologists like John and ReBecca Foster continue to consider Brontosaurus a synonym of Apatosaurus.
facts.quote: Some paleontologists, such as John and ReBecca Foster, continue to consider Brontosaurus as a synonym of Apatosaurus.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus was a large, quadrupedal animal with a long neck, a whip-like tail, and forelimbs shorter than its hindlimbs.
facts.quote: Brontosaurus was a large, long-necked, quadrupedal animal with a long, whip-like tail, and forelimbs that were slightly shorter than its hindlimbs.

facts.statement: The largest species, B. excelsus, grew up to 23 meters long and weighed up to 20 tons, while other species reached 19 meters and 14 tons.
facts.quote: The largest species, B. excelsus, measured up to 21 - 23 m long from head to tail and weighed up to 15 - 20 t; other species were smaller, measuring 19 m long and weighing 14 MT.

facts.statement: The skull of Brontosaurus has never been found, so scientists believe it was similar to that of the closely related Apatosaurus.
facts.quote: Although the skull of Brontosaurus has not been found, it was probably similar to the skull of the closely related Apatosaurus.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus possessed chisel-like teeth adapted for eating plants, similar to those of its relative Apatosaurus.
facts.quote: Jaws of Apatosaurus and other diplodocids were lined with spatulate (chisel-like) teeth which were adapted for herbivory.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus had a wide and deep neck formed by vertebrae with paired spines on their upper surface.
facts.quote: Like those of other diplodocids, the vertebrae of the neck were deeply bifurcated on the dorsal side; that is, they carried paired spines, resulting in a wide and deep neck.

facts.statement: Large air holes in the neck, torso, and sacrum vertebrae helped lighten Brontosaurus's bones to support its massive size.
facts.quote: Vertebrae in the neck, torso, and sacrum of sauropods bore large pneumatic foramina on their lateral sides. These are used to lighten the bones which aided in keeping the animal lighter.

facts.statement: Despite being filled with air pockets, the neck of Brontosaurus was estimated to be twice as heavy as the necks of other diplodocids because it was much sturdier.
facts.quote: Despite its pneumaticy, the neck of Brontosaurus is thought to have been double the mass of that of other diplodocids due to the former's sturdiness.

facts.statement: Specimens of Brontosaurus parvus show that the tail had an extensive air-sac system designed to reduce weight.
facts.quote: The tail also bears an extensive air-sac system to lighten its weight, as observed in specimens of B. parvus.

facts.statement: The end of Brontosaurus's tail had a whip-like structure, a feature shared with other diplodocids.
facts.quote: As in other diplodocids, the last portion of the tail of Brontosaurus possessed a whip-like structure.

facts.statement: A depression on the back of the shoulder blade distinguishes Brontosaurus from Apatosaurus, which lacks this feature.
facts.quote: One of the traits that distinguishes Brontosaurus and Apatosaurus is the presence of a depression on the posterior face of the scapula, which the latter lacks.

facts.statement: A rounded extension on the edge of the shoulder blade is a unique characteristic of Brontosaurus among the Apatosaurinae subfamily.
facts.quote: The scapula of Brontosaurus also has a rounded extension off of its edge, a characteristic unique to Brontosaurus among Apatosaurinae.

facts.statement: In 1936, Charles Gilmore corrected earlier reconstructions, noting that Brontosaurus's forearm bones remained parallel rather than crossing.
facts.quote: Charles Gilmore in 1936 noted that previous reconstructions erroneously proposed that the radius and ulna could cross, when in life they would have remained parallel.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus had only one large claw on each forelimb that faced inward, while the other fingers lacked claws.
facts.quote: Brontosaurus had a single large claw on each forelimb which faced towards the body, whereas the rest of the phalanges lacked unguals.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus had a foot with three claws on the innermost toe, following a digit formula of 3-4-5-3-2.
facts.quote: The foot of Brontosaurus has three claws on the innermost digits; the digit formula is 3-4-5-3-2.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus belongs to the family Diplodocidae, a group of gigantic sauropod dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Brontosaurus is a member of the family Diplodocidae, a clade of gigantic sauropod dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus is classified within the subfamily Apatosaurinae, which also includes Apatosaurus and potentially other unnamed genera.
facts.quote: Brontosaurus is classified in the subfamily Apatosaurinae, which also includes Apatosaurus and possibly one or more unnamed genera.

facts.statement: A 2015 study by a British-Portuguese team concluded that Brontosaurus is a valid genus distinct from Apatosaurus.
facts.quote: However, an extensive study published in 2015 by a joint British-Portuguese research team concluded that Brontosaurus was a valid genus of sauropod distinct from Apatosaurus.

facts.statement: Not all paleontologists agree with the conclusion that Brontosaurus is a distinct genus from Apatosaurus.
facts.quote: Nevertheless, not all paleontologists agree with this division.

facts.statement: The family Diplodocidae, to which Brontosaurus belongs, first evolved in the Middle Jurassic in what is now Georgia before spreading across North America in the Late Jurassic.
facts.quote: Diplodocids first evolved during the Middle Jurassic in what is now Georgia, spreading to North America during the Late Jurassic.

facts.statement: The species Brontosaurus excelsus was first named by Othniel Marsh in 1879.
facts.quote: Brontosaurus excelsus, the type species of Brontosaurus, was first named by Marsh in 1879.

facts.statement: The species Brontosaurus parvus was originally described as Elosaurus in 1902 by Peterson and Gilmore before being moved to the genus Brontosaurus in 2015.
facts.quote: Brontosaurus parvus, first described as Elosaurus in 1902 by Peterson and Gilmore, was reassigned to Apatosaurus in 1994, and to Brontosaurus in 2015.

facts.statement: Definitive fossils of B. excelsus come from Wyoming and date to about 152 million years ago during the late Kimmeridgian age.
facts.quote: The known definitive B. excelsus fossils have been reported from Reed's Quarries 10 and 11 of the Morrison Formation Brushy Basin member in Albany County, Wyoming, dated to the late Kimmeridgian age, about 152 million years ago.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus yahnahpin is the oldest known species, dating to about 155 million years ago.
facts.quote: Brontosaurus yahnahpin is the oldest species, known from a single site from the lower Morrison Formation, Bertha Quarry, in Albany County, Wyoming, dating to about 155 million years ago.

facts.statement: The largest known specimens of B. excelsus could reach a length of 22 meters and weigh up to 15 tonnes.
facts.quote: The largest of these specimens is estimated to have weighed up to 15 tonnes and measured up to 22 m long from head to tail.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus yahnahpin grew to a maximum length of 21 meters.
facts.quote: It grew up to 21 m long.

facts.statement: Trackways indicate Brontosaurus could travel an average of 20 to 40 km per day and reach speeds of 20 to 30 km/h.
facts.quote: Trackways of sauropods like Brontosaurus show that the average range for them was around 20 - 40 km per day, and they could potentially reach a top speed of 20 - 30 km/h.

facts.statement: The single forelimb claw of Brontosaurus was likely used for grasping tree trunks while rearing up to feed, rather than for defense or foraging.
facts.quote: Various uses for the single claw on the forelimb of sauropods have been proposed. One suggestion is that they were used for defense, but their shape and size make this unlikely. It was also possible they were for foraging, but the most probable use for the claw was grasping objects such as tree trunks when rearing.

facts.statement: Recent evidence suggests Brontosaurus was a fully terrestrial animal, contradicting older theories that it lived partly submerged in water.
facts.quote: Recent findings do not support this, and sauropods are thought to have been fully terrestrial animals.

facts.statement: Research suggests Brontosaurus likely possessed an avian-style respiratory system to help regulate body heat.
facts.quote: Matt Wedel found that an avian system would have allowed them to dump more heat.

facts.statement: It is debated whether juvenile Apatosaurus, and by extension Brontosaurus, could walk on two legs based on disputed trackway evidence.
facts.quote: A possible bipedal trackway of a juvenile Apatosaurus is known, but it is disputed if it was possible for the sauropod.

facts.statement: Scientists debate the exact metabolic requirements of Brontosaurus due to a lack of modern animal analogues.
facts.quote: Hypotheses of the food requirements of Brontosaurus have been made, though predicting this is difficult due to the lack of modern analogues.

facts.statement: The famous skeleton at the Field Museum of Natural History was once assigned to Brontosaurus but is now considered an unknown species of apatosaurine.
facts.quote: Many specimens have been assigned to the species, such as FMNH P25112, the skeleton mounted at the Field Museum of Natural History, which has since been found to represent an unknown species of apatosaurine.

facts.statement: An alternative method estimated Brontosaurus grew 520 kg per year and reached full mass before about 70 years old.
facts.quote: An alternative method, using limb length and body mass, found Brontosaurus and Apatosaurus grew 520 kg per year, and reached their full mass before it was about 70 years old.

facts.statement: Some researchers consider growth rate estimates unreliable because old growth lines may have been obliterated by bone remodeling.
facts.quote: These estimates have been called unreliable because the calculation methods are not sound; old growth lines would have been obliterated by bone remodeling.

facts.statement: The number of sacral vertebrae, increasing to five at maturity, was one of the first identified growth factors for Apatosaurus.
facts.quote: One of the first identified growth factors of Apatosaurus was the number of sacral vertebrae, which increased to five by the time of the creature's maturity.

facts.statement: Peterson and Gilmore theorized that sauropods never stopped growing to attain massive size, a concept unsupported by fossil evidence.
facts.quote: Peterson and Gilmore also theorized that sauropods never stopped growing, which supposedly helped in attaining their massive size, a concept unsupported by fossils.

facts.statement: Computer simulations suggest the long, tapering tail of Brontosaurus resembled a bullwhip.
facts.quote: Myhrvold carried out a computer simulation of the tail, which in diplodocids like Brontosaurus was a very long, tapering structure resembling a [bullwhip.

facts.statement: Modeling suggested Brontosaurus could produce a tail-cracking sound of over 200 decibels, comparable to a cannon.
facts.quote: This computer modeling suggested that sauropods were capable of producing a whip-like cracking sound of over 200 decibels, comparable to the volume of a cannon.

facts.statement: Rega (2012) argues against the tail-whip hypothesis, noting similar vertebral fusion in Camarasaurus and Mamenchisaurus despite them lacking tailwhips.
facts.quote: However, Rega (2012) notes that Camarasaurus while lacking a tailwhip, displays a similar level of caudal co-ossification and that Mamenchisaurus while having the same pattern of vertebral metrics, lacks a tailwhip and does not display fusion in any "transitional region".

facts.statement: Baron (2020) considers the tail-whip hypothesis unlikely due to the risk of catastrophic muscle and skeletal damage from such speeds.
facts.quote: More recently, Baron (2020) has considered the use of the tail as a bullwhip unlikely because of the potentially catastrophic muscle and skeletal damage such speeds could cause on the large and heavy tail.

facts.statement: The robust cervical vertebrae of Brontosaurus had expensive energy requirements, suggesting their evolution served an important function.
facts.quote: These structures had expensive energy requirements, so the reason for their evolution must have been important to the animal.

facts.statement: Round protruding processes on the ventral sides of cervical ribs have been suggested to be attachment points for bosses or keratinous spikes.
facts.quote: These have been suggested to have been attachment points for bosses or keratinous spikes.

facts.statement: A 2015 preprint suggested Brontosaurus used its neck for combat between individuals through striking.
facts.quote: A preprint by Wedel et al (2015) thought that due to the combination of these traits, Brontosaurus would use its neck for combat between individuals through the use of striking necks.

facts.statement: The Morrison Formation, where Brontosaurus lived, dates from 156.3 to 146.8 million years ago, spanning the Late Jurassic period.
facts.quote: The Morrison Formation is a sequence of shallow marine and alluvial sediments which, according to radiometric dating, ranges between 156.3 million years old (Mya) at its base, and 146.8 Mya at the top, which places it in the late Oxfordian, Kimmeridgian, and early Tithonian stages of the Late Jurassic period.

facts.statement: The Morrison Formation environment is interpreted as semi-arid with distinct wet and dry seasons.
facts.quote: This formation is interpreted as a semi-arid environment with distinct wet and dry seasons.

facts.statement: The Morrison Basin stretched from New Mexico to Alberta and Saskatchewan, formed by the uplift of the Rocky Mountains.
facts.quote: The Morrison Basin, where dinosaurs lived, stretched from New Mexico to Alberta and Saskatchewan and was formed when the precursors to the Front Range of the Rocky Mountains started pushing up to the west.

facts.statement: Fossils of B. excelsus date to the late Kimmeridgian age, about 151 million years ago.
facts.quote: B. excelsus fossils have been reported from only the Brushy Basin Member, dating to the late Kimmeridgian age, about 151 Mya.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus fossils have been found in Wyoming, Colorado, Oklahoma, and Utah within stratigraphic zones 2–6.
facts.quote: Fossils of these animals have been found in Nine Mile Quarry and Bone Cabin Quarry in Wyoming and at sites in Colorado, Oklahoma, and Utah, present in stratigraphic zones 2–6 according to John Foster's model.

facts.statement: The Morrison Formation records an environment dominated by gigantic sauropod dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The Morrison Formation records an environment and time dominated by gigantic sauropod dinosaurs.

facts.statement: The flora of the period included green algae, mosses, horsetails, cycads, ginkgoes, and conifers.
facts.quote: The flora of the period has been revealed by fossils of green algae, mosses, horsetails, cycads, ginkgoes, and several families of conifers.

facts.statement: A 1925 silent film depicted a Brontosaurus fighting an Allosaurus using special effects created by Willis O'Brien.
facts.quote: The 1925 silent film The Lost World featured a battle between a Brontosaurus and an Allosaurus, using special effects by Willis O'Brien.

facts.statement: The assembly of a Brontosaurus skeleton served as a major plot point in the 1938 film Bringing Up Baby.
facts.quote: In 1938 the assembling of a Brontosaurus skeleton was a major plot point in the Katharine Hepburn and Cary Grant film Bringing Up Baby.

facts.statement: The U.S. Postal Service issued Brontosaurus stamps in 1989, sparking controversy over the use of the name instead of the scientific Apatosaurus.
facts.quote: As late as 1989, the U.S. Postal Service faced controversy when it issued four "dinosaur" stamps: Tyrannosaurus, Stegosaurus, Pteranodon, and Brontosaurus.

facts.statement: The genus Brontosaurus was originally named by its discoverer Othniel Charles Marsh in 1879.
facts.quote: Brontosaurus fue originalmente nombrado por su descubridor Othniel Charles Marsh en 1879.

facts.statement: A comprehensive study published in 2015 concluded that Brontosaurus is a valid genus distinct from Apatosaurus.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, un extenso estudio publicado en 2015 concluyó que Brontosaurus es un género válido de saurópodo y distinto de Apatosaurus.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic period, approximately 155 to 152 million years ago, in North America.
facts.quote: vivió a finales del periodo Jurásico hace aproximadamente entre 155 a 152 millones de años en la época del Kimmeridgiense de Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus species lived between 155 and 152 million years ago in the lower to middle Morrison Formation of Wyoming and Utah.
facts.quote: Las especies de Brontosaurus se extienden en un rango temporal de 155 a 152 millones de años, durante la época del Kimmeridgiense de la zona inferior a media de la Formación Morrison en Wyoming y Utah, en Estados Unidos.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus was a large quadrupedal animal with a long neck and a long whip-like tail.
facts.quote: Brontosaurus era un animal cuadrúpedo grande dotado de un cuello largo y larga cola en forma de látigo.

facts.statement: The largest species, B. excelsus, weighed over 15 tonnes and measured more than 22 meters in length from head to tail.
facts.quote: La especie más grande, B. excelsus, pesaba más de 15 toneladas y medía más de 22 metros de longitud de la cabeza a la cola.

facts.statement: The neck possessed an extensive system of air sacs that lightened its weight.
facts.quote: El cuello poseía un extenso sistema de sacos aéreos que lo aligeraban.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus had very long ribs compared to many other diplodocids, giving them unusually high torsos.
facts.quote: Brontosaurus además tenían costillas muy largas comparadas con muchos otros diplodócidos, lo que les daba torsos inusualmente altos.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus had a single large claw on each front foot, while only the first three toes on its hind feet had claws.
facts.quote: Brontosaurus tenía una única gran garra en cada pata delantera, mientras que en su pie solo los primeros tres dedos tenían garras.

facts.statement: The genus Brontosaurus was established by Marsh in 1879.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Marsh, 1879

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Brontosaurus is Brontosaurus excelsus.
facts.quote: type_species: Brontosaurus excelsus

facts.statement: Two species are recognized within the genus: Brontosaurus parvus, described in 1902, and Brontosaurus yahnahpin, described in 1994.
facts.quote: subdivision: Brontosaurus parvus (, 1902) Brontosaurus yahnahpin (, 1994)

facts.statement: Historical synonyms for Brontosaurus include Elosaurus (Peterson & Gilmore, 1902) and Eobrontosaurus (Bakker, 1998).
facts.quote: synonyms: Elosaurus Peterson & Gilmore, 1902 Eobrontosaurus Bakker, 1998

facts.statement: The use of the name Brontosaurus instead of Apatosaurus led to complaints that it fostered scientific illiteracy.
facts.quote: The use of the term Brontosaurus in place of Apatosaurus led to complaints of "fostering scientific illiteracy."

facts.statement: Paleontologist Stephen Jay Gould supported the use of Brontosaurus on stamps despite scientific inaccuracy, arguing that no one complained about the use of Pteranodon, which is not a true dinosaur.
facts.quote: Palaeontologist Stephen Jay Gould supported this position. In the essay from which the title of the 1991 collection Bully for Brontosaurus is taken, Gould wrote: "Touché and right on; no one bitched about Pteranodon, and that's a real error."

facts.statement: A study by Tschopp regarding the validity of Brontosaurus generated a high volume of responses from opposing groups worldwide.
facts.quote: Tschopp's study has generated a very high number of responses from many, often opposed, groups—of editorial, news staff, and personal blog nature (both related and not), from both sides of the debate, from related and unrelated contexts, and from all over the world.

facts.statement: Othniel C. Marsh discovered a large, fairly complete sauropod skeleton in Como Bluff, Wyoming, in 1879.
facts.quote: En 1879, Othniel C. Marsh, un profesor de paleontología de la Universidad de Yale, anunció el descubrimiento de un esqueleto de un saurópodo grande y bastante completo de rocas de la Formación Morrison en Como Bluff, Wyoming.

facts.statement: Marsh named the new genus and species Brontosaurus excelsus, meaning "thunder lizard" in Greek and "noble" or "high" in Latin.
facts.quote: Lo identificó como perteneciente a un género y especie completamente nuevos, a los que nombró como Brontosaurus excelsus, que significa "lagarto trueno", del griego brontē/βροντη que significa "trueno" y sauros/σαυρος que significa "lagarto", y el latín excelsus, "noble" o "alto".

facts.statement: Publications and descriptions of taxa by Marsh and Cope were made hastily due to their fossil collecting competition.
facts.quote: Por lo tanto, las publicaciones y descripciones de los taxones hechas por Marsh y Cope fueron hechas de manera apresurada.

facts.statement: In 1903, Elmer Riggs argued that Brontosaurus was not distinct enough from Apatosaurus to warrant its own genus, creating the new combination Apatosaurus excelsus.
facts.quote: Elmer Riggs, en la edición de 1903 de la revista Geological Series of the Field Columbian Museum, afirmó que Brontosaurus no era lo bastante distinto de Apatosaurus como para garantizar su propio género, por lo que creó la nueva combinación Apatosaurus excelsus.

facts.statement: The American Museum of Natural History unveiled the first mounted sauropod skeleton in 1905, a composite specimen mostly formed from bones of AMNH 460 referred to as Brontosaurus excelsus.
facts.quote: En 1905, el Museo Americano de Historia Natural (AMNH) reveló el primer esqueleto montado de un saurópodo, un espécimen compuesto, mayormente formado de los huesos de AMNH 460, que fue referido a la especie Brontosaurus excelsus.

facts.statement: To complete the mount, the rest of the tail was modeled to look like Marsh believed it should have been, with very few vertebrae.
facts.quote: Para completar la montura, el resto de la cola fue modelada para que tuviera la apariencia que Marsh creía debía tener, la cual tenía muy pocas vértebras.

facts.statement: A sculpted model representing what museum authorities thought the skull of the creature should look like was placed on the skeleton.
facts.quote: Además de esto, se colocó en el esqueleto un modelo esculpido de como pensaban las autoridades del museo que debía ser el cráneo de la inmensa criatura.

facts.statement: The skull model was not a delicate one like Diplodocus but was based on larger, thicker, and stronger cranial bones, jaws, and dental crowns from three different quarries.
facts.quote: Este no era un cráneo delicado como el de Diplodocus, el cual más tarde se mostraría que es más correcto, sino que estaba basado en "los huesos craneales, mandíbulas y coronas dentales más grandes, gruesas y fuertes de tres canteras diferentes".

facts.statement: Adam Hermann was forced to hand-carve a replacement skull because he could not find Brontosaurus skulls.
facts.quote: Hermann fue forzado a esculpir a mano un reemplazo.

facts.statement: Henry Fairfield Osborn noted in a publication that the skull was mostly a conjecture based on Morosaurus, now known as Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: Henry Fairfield Osborn señaló en una publicación que el cráneo era "mayormente una conjetura y basado en el de Morosaurus", ahora Camarasaurus.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus is a member of the family Diplodocidae, a clade of gigantic sauropod dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Brontosaurus es un miembro de la familia Diplodocidae, un clado de gigantescos dinosaurios saurópodos.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus is also classified in the subfamily Apatosaurinae, which includes Apatosaurus and one or more possible unnamed genera.
facts.quote: Brontosaurus es además clasificado en la subfamilia Apatosaurinae, la cual también incluye a Apatosaurus y uno o más posibles géneros aún sin nombrar.

facts.statement: A 2015 study by a British-Portuguese research team concluded that Brontosaurus is a valid sauropod genus distinct from Apatosaurus.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, un extenso estudio publicado en 2015 por el equipo de investigación conjunto británico-portugués concluyó que Brontosaurus era un género de saurópodo válido y distinto de Apatosaurus.

facts.statement: However, not all paleontologists agree with this division.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, no todos los paleontólogos están de acuerdo con esta división.

facts.statement: Specimens of B. excelsus have been reported from the Reed's 10 quarry in the Brushy Basin member of the Morrison Formation in Albany County, Wyoming, dating to the late Kimmeridgian, about 152 million years ago.
facts.quote: Estos especímenes pertenecientes a B. excelsus han sido reportados de la Cantera Reed's 10 del miembro Brushy Basin de la Formación Morrison en el Condado de Albany (Wyoming), que datan de finales de la época del Kimeridgiano, hace unos 152 millones de años.

facts.statement: The largest specimens of B. excelsus are estimated to have weighed over 15 tons and measured over 22 meters in body length.
facts.quote: Se estima que el mayor de estos especímenes habría pesado más de 15 toneladas y medía más de 22 metros de longitud corporal.

facts.statement: Specimens of B. parvus date to the middle Kimmeridgian.
facts.quote: Data de mediados del Kimeridgiano.

facts.statement: Adult specimens of B. parvus are estimated to have weighed over 14 tons and measured over 22 meters in body length.
facts.quote: Se estima que los especímenes adultos pesaban más de 14 toneladas y medían más de 22 metros de longitud corporal.

facts.statement: Brontosaurus yahnahpin is the oldest known species, found at a single site in the lower zone of the Morrison Formation at Bertha Quarry in Albany County, Wyoming, dating to about 155 million years ago.
facts.quote: Brontosaurus yahnahpin es la especie más antigua, conocida de un único sitio de la zona inferior de la Formación Morrison, en la Cantera Bertha en el Condado de Albany, Wyoming, datando de hace unos 155 millones de años.

facts.statement: B. yahnahpin reached a length of 21 meters.
facts.quote: Llegaba a medir 21 metros de largo.

facts.statement: The species name derives from the Lakota term mah-koo yah-nah-pin, meaning "breast collar," referencing a pair of sternum ribs resembling bone vests traditionally worn by the tribe.
facts.quote: El nombre de la especie se deriva del término lakota mah-koo yah-nah-pin, "collar de pecho", una referencia al par de costillas del esternón que recuerdan a las pecheras de hueso vestidas tradicionalmente por la tribu.

facts.statement: A 1998 re-evaluation by Robert T. Bakker determined it was more primitive, leading Bakker to coin the new genus name Eobrontosaurus, derived from the Greek word eos, meaning "dawn," added to Brontosaurus.
facts.quote: Una revaluación hecha por Robert T. Bakker en 1998 determinó que era más primitivo, por lo que Bakker acuñó el nuevo nombre de género Eobrontosaurus, derivado del término griego eos, "amanecer", añadido a Brontosaurus.

facts.statement: Historically, it was thought that sauropods like Brontosaurus were too large to support their own weight on land and likely lived partially submerged in water or swamps.
facts.quote: Históricamente, se pensaba que saurópodos como Brontosaurus eran demasiado grandes como para soportar su propio peso en tierra firme, por lo que teóricamente debieron de vivir al menos parcialmente sumergidos en agua, quizás en pantanos.

facts.statement: Recent findings do not support the aquatic theory, and evidence now points to sauropods being fully terrestrial animals.
facts.quote: Los hallazgos recientes no apoyan esa idea, y en cambio la evidencia apunta a que los saurópodos eran animales completamente terrestres.

facts.statement: Diplodocids like Brontosaurus are frequently depicted holding their necks in an upright position to eat from tall trees.
facts.quote: Con frecuencia, los diplodócidos como Brontosaurus se los representa manteniendo sus cuellos en una posición erguida, permitiéndoles comer de árboles altos.

facts.statement: Sauropod trackways show Brontosaurus could travel an average of 20-40 km per day and potentially reach a maximum speed of 20-30 km per hour.
facts.quote: Los rastros de huellas de saurópodos como Brontosaurus muestran que podían recorrer en promedio 20-40 km al día, y que podían potencialmente alcanzar una velocidad máxima de 20-30 km por hora.

facts.statement: It has been suggested that the unique front claw was used for defense, but its shape and size make this unlikely.
facts.quote: Se ha sugerido que se usaban para la defensa, pero su forma y tamaño hace esto improbable.

facts.statement: While some suggest the claw was used for feeding, it is most likely used for grasping objects like tree trunks when standing upright.
facts.quote: Otra idea es que usaban para la alimentación, pero lo más probable es que la garra fuera usada para aprehender objetos como los troncos de árboles al erguirse.

facts.statement: The genus Brontosaurus belongs to the parent group Apatosaurinae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Apatosaurinae

facts.statement: Brontosaurus is classified in the family Diplodocidae.
facts.quote: Family: Diplodocidae

facts.statement: Brontosaurus belongs to the class Saurischia.
facts.quote: Class: Saurischia

facts.statement: Brontosaurus lived from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian stages, between 154.8 and 143.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Kimmeridgian to Tithonian (154.8 to 143.1 million years ago)
